profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at an international law faculty research center between the lead investigator of a new empirical project and the center's research counsel-methodologist. They are preparing a 10-week work plan for a report that will empirically assess common claims about investment treaty arbitration using publicly available awards, procedural orders, institutional summaries, and treaty text. The agenda is to decide the dataset boundaries, assign coding responsibilities, set the timeline for a first draft, and align on what the 'case list,' 'award data,' and 'cost figures' deliverables will include. The expected outcome is a shared project plan covering source collection, coding, quality review, and drafting responsibilities for a publishable working paper intended for policy audiences and academic submission.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marceau
members.role: Principal Investigator and Professor of International Investment Law
members.expertise: investment treaty arbitration, treaty interpretation, public international law scholarship
members.background: Elena is a tenured law professor who has written doctrinal pieces on investor-state dispute settlement and now wants to produce a methodologically transparent empirical article with policy relevance. She has supervised prior research assistants on arbitral award coding but has not herself run a large reproducible dataset project.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, defensible study that can be drafted quickly enough to circulate before an upcoming treaty reform workshop, and she is especially concerned about not overpromising data completeness where awards and cost information are fragmented.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case' in this project means a distinct arbitration proceeding that reached a publicly traceable procedural endpoint, even if damages or annulment generated separate later decisions.
When the team says 'award data,' the practical unit is merits or final award information sufficient to code outcome and amounts, not every procedural or post-award decision.
A 'first draft' means a draft with core descriptive tables and caveated placeholders for sparse variables like costs, suitable for internal circulation and workshop discussion.
Coding 'other dispute resolution processes' includes only pre- or parallel formal mechanisms clearly referenced in the award record, not informal settlement efforts unless documented in the decision.

members.name: Samuel Ortiz
members.role: Research Counsel and Empirical Methods Lead
members.expertise: empirical legal methods, litigation datasets, coding protocols, reproducibility and source auditing
members.background: Samuel is a former arbitration associate who moved into empirical legal research administration. He designs codebooks, trains student coders, and emphasizes audit trails, version control, and decision rules that can withstand replication scrutiny.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid a dataset that looks polished but is impossible to replicate later, and he is trying to build a workflow that junior coders can execute consistently without constant professor intervention.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case' should be the docket-level dispute family, so related jurisdiction, merits, damages, annulment, and rectification decisions remain linked under one master matter unless explicitly split for analysis later.
When the team says 'award data,' every award-type instrument that affects the dispute record should be logged because later analyses may depend on procedural sequence and publication patterns.
A 'first draft' means a near-submission-quality evidence package with stable tables, documented coding rules, and resolved source discrepancies rather than a narrative placeholder draft.

If the study mentions costs or use of other dispute resolution processes, the coding protocol should actively search party memorials, institutional summaries, and secondary databases where awards are silent, so the variable is not undercounted by design.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to finalize the 'case list' before coding begins.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a list of individual arbitration proceedings with one row per publicly identifiable proceeding ending in a merits, jurisdictional, settlement-linked discontinuance, or similar endpoint.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a master list of dispute matters where all linked decisions and post-award stages are grouped under one docket-family entry with sub-records to be expanded later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In empirical legal projects, 'case list' sounds routine and both views are professionally reasonable; because both anticipate spreadsheets with linked records, neither notices they are defining the basic unit differently.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that student coders will start extracting 'award data' in week three.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects coders to capture merits outcomes, damages claimed and awarded, tribunal composition, and any cost figures from final or merits-related awards only.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects coders to log jurisdictional awards, partial awards, annulment decisions, rectification decisions, and procedural decisions that materially affect publication status or sequence, even if they do not contain damages.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using a familiar umbrella phrase and both assume the other knows that the exact inclusion logic follows naturally from the project's topic; the difference concerns second-order boundaries, not the obvious core variables.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the first draft should be ready by the end of week eight.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks success means a readable internal manuscript with provisional tables, caveats on missingness, and enough analysis to discuss at the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks success means a vetted draft whose tables are frozen, coding exceptions resolved, and appendix-ready methodology complete enough that no major data architecture changes remain.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Planning meetings routinely use milestone labels like 'first draft' without unpacking quality thresholds; both hear a standard project checkpoint and assume their interpretation is the common academic norm.

misalignment_points.topic: How to code costs and other dispute resolution processes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to capture 'cost figures and use of other dispute resolution processes' where available.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes coders will record these variables only when explicitly stated in publicly available awards or decisions, preserving a conservative and easily defensible evidentiary base.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes coders will supplement the record by consulting institutional digests, party summaries, memorial excerpts, and established secondary databases to infer or document these variables when awards are incomplete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse methodological rigor and transparency, so the procedural gap hides beneath shared language about capturing information 'where available'; each assumes availability obviously includes the sources they normally rely on.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to become a credible, policy-relevant paper fast, not a sprawling database exercise. The project should assess the standard claims people keep making about investment treaty arbitration, but on a transparent basis that I can defend at the workshop. The case list has to be workable: one row per distinct arbitration proceeding with a publicly traceable endpoint, so we are not endlessly debating how to treat later damages, annulment, or rectification phases as if they were the same observational unit. And when I say first draft, I mean something readable and useful for internal circulation by week eight, even if some variables, especially costs, remain patchy and clearly caveated.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want this report to be a transparent empirical assessment of the recurring claims about investment treaty arbitration, but we need a plan that is actually workable over ten weeks. So I think today's priorities are to settle the case list, map the coding sequence, and make sure the first draft is realistically timed.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If we do not lock structure early, the students will create a mess that cannot be audited later. For me, the case list has to be the master matter list at the docket-family level, with linked instruments nested underneath. That way jurisdiction, merits, annulment, rectification, and anything else stay attached to the same dispute history. If Elena wants policy-facing output, all the more reason to make the architecture clean from the start so we do not retrofit provenance afterward.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I would strongly prefer that we lock the case list first, because the coding protocol will be much cleaner if it's built around a stable record structure from the outset. That also gives us a proper audit trail downstream instead of trying to reconstruct one after the fact.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: we need the proceedings identified and then move. End of week two for the case list seems sensible if we keep the unit tight and practical. By week three the students can begin extracting award data from the merits or final awards that actually let us code outcomes, claimed amounts, awarded amounts, and tribunal composition. Arbitrator nationality and gender are feasible, and they matter for the claims people care about. I do not want us held up waiting for every stray procedural document.
turns.utterance: My instinct is that the case list should be completed by the end of week two. Then in week three the student coders can begin extracting award data, starting with the variables we know we'll need for outcomes, amounts, and tribunal characteristics like nationality and gender.

turns.inner_thought: That sequencing works, as long as award data is understood broadly enough to preserve the dispute record. Once the students start, they should log every award-type instrument that matters to sequence and status—jurisdictional decisions, partial awards, annulment, rectification, maybe even publication-relevant procedural instruments where they affect what is observable. If we skip those now, later reproducibility will be painful and we will not be able to explain why a dispute appears the way it does.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. And once award data extraction starts, I'd like the team to log linked jurisdictional, partial, annulment, and rectification decisions as they encounter them, so the later analysis is easier to reproduce and we don't have to backfill the record.

turns.inner_thought: What I need in the paper is straightforward: tables on claimant win-loss rates, amounts claimed and awarded, and whatever cost figures are available from the public decisions. If costs are missing, we simply say they are missing. The first draft does not need methodological perfection; it needs a coherent manuscript with the main descriptive tables and clear caveats so I can circulate it before the workshop. I must not overstate completeness where the underlying awards are fragmented.
turns.utterance: On the substance, the first draft should already contain the core tables people will expect: win-loss rates, amounts claimed and awarded, and whatever cost figures are available. If we can get those in shape early, the rest of the narrative becomes much easier to write.

turns.inner_thought: If those tables are going into a first draft, they need to be durable enough that we are not rewriting them later because of avoidable undercounting. Costs and other dispute resolution processes are classic examples where awards alone are incomplete. We should actively search institutional summaries, secondary databases, and any accessible companion materials so the variables are not sparse by design. For me, first draft means the evidence package is already stabilized enough to survive serious scrutiny.
turns.utterance: I agree on the timing for the first draft. To make those tables hold up, though, I think the coders should capture cost figures and use of other dispute resolution processes where available, including from institutional summaries and secondary sources when the awards themselves are thin.

turns.inner_thought: I do want Samuel to run the codebook because he is much better at coder training and protocol discipline. But I need the rules to stay anchored to what is actually documented in the public award record; that keeps the methodology clean and prevents us from making inferential leaps that are hard to defend to legal readers. Award data, in my mind, is still the information sufficient to code the proceeding's outcome and amounts, not every document orbiting the dispute.
turns.utterance: That works. Why don't you take the lead on the codebook and the student instructions. I would just like the coding rules to stay closely tied to what is documented in the public award record, so the methodology section remains straightforward and easy to defend.

turns.inner_thought: Fine—I'll make provenance explicit so nothing is hidden. If Elena wants defensibility, the best answer is not to avoid companion materials but to document them carefully. I'll create source fields that distinguish the award itself from institutional summaries, databases, or other companion records. And because my case architecture is matter-based, each case entry can carry sub-records and notes showing where every figure came from without losing linkage across decisions.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll set it up so the source fields and provenance notes are explicit, and each case can show which figures came from the award itself and which came from companion materials. That should keep the process transparent without making the spreadsheet unwieldy.

turns.inner_thought: Week eight is still the right target. By then I want a readable draft with the core tables in place and a narrative that openly explains publication gaps, missing cost information, and any obvious limitations. We can refine and deepen after the workshop, but I need something coherent enough to circulate internally. I do not need every discrepancy eliminated before there is text on the page.
turns.utterance: Good. I think week eight should still be enough for the first draft, provided the core tables are in place and the narrative can simply explain any gaps in publication or missing costs. For this stage, clarity about limits is more important than pretending the record is complete.

turns.inner_thought: Week eight is feasible only if week seven is protected for data stabilization. With a matter-level case list, duplicate records and linked decisions are exactly where student coding usually goes wrong. I need one full week to reconcile identifiers, resolve discrepancies across sub-records, and make sure the tables are not shifting under us. Otherwise the so-called first draft will just be a temporary snapshot rather than a reliable analytical product.
turns.utterance: That timeline works for me, as long as we reserve week seven for resolving duplicate records and checking linked decisions inside each matter before the first draft is assembled. If we do that cleanup late, the tables should be much more stable.

turns.inner_thought: He's thinking carefully about structure, which is useful. As long as it doesn't slow the main paper, that's fine. I will refine the substantive framing and make sure the research questions stay trained on the claims that policy audiences care about. Meanwhile, once the case list is settled, the students can move directly into award data extraction for the awards that let us code the key variables. That should keep momentum and get us to a draft by week eight.
turns.utterance: All right, then let me summarize. I'll refine the substantive research questions and start sketching the paper's argument, and you'll build the coding spreadsheet and codebook. Once the case list is settled, the students can begin with the award data and we can review the first wave together.

turns.inner_thought: That gives me enough to proceed. I'll circulate a protocol that includes source logging, coding rules, and the provenance structure for costs and other dispute resolution processes, plus a draft outline for the manuscript. If I can get buy-in early next week, the team can move quickly without sacrificing replicability. Elena sounds comfortable, so she is probably imagining roughly the same workflow I am.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll circulate the protocol, the source log template, and a proposed structure for the first draft by early next week. That should give everyone a clear work plan on collection, coding, review, and writing before the students begin.
